title: Multi-Step Workflows and Agents — Module Quiz

items.q: What separates a workflow from an agent?
options: Whether a language model is involved at all
Who decides the next step: you in advance, or the model at run time
How many tools are connected to the system
items.explain: A workflow's path is fixed and readable before it runs. In an agent the model decides it from what it has seen so far, so the route is discovered.

items.q: A refund process has four fixed steps and one judgement call. How should it be built?
options: As an agent, because a judgement call is involved
As a workflow with a model in the one step that needs judgement
As an agent, to leave room for unusual refund cases
items.explain: You keep the exactness of the fixed steps and confine the unpredictability to the one place it belongs.

items.q: Why is an agent's failure often harder to place than a chain's?
options: Agents produce no logs
The fault may be a choice many turns earlier that looked reasonable when it was made
Agents run on separate infrastructure from chains
items.explain: In a chain you know which step broke. In an agent the route is discovered, so the cause can sit far from where the symptom appeared.

items.q: When should an existing workflow step be promoted into a loop?
options: When the team wants the system to feel more capable
Only when you can state why a fixed branch cannot do the job
As soon as the workflow has more than five steps
items.explain: If you cannot state it, it is a workflow. Promote only the step that genuinely needs a choice, and keep the rest exact.

items.q: Mechanically, what is an agent?
options: A model with persistent memory of earlier conversations
A model in a loop: choose a tool or finish, run it, add the result to the history, repeat
A group of cooperating models, each responsible for a single task
items.explain: The apparent intelligence belongs to the model, but the structure is a while loop. Seeing it plainly makes the costs easy to predict.

items.q: Why does a twenty-turn run cost far more than twice a ten-turn run?
options: Later turns use more expensive models
Each turn re-sends the whole history, which is longer every time, so the total grows roughly with the square of the turns
Providers charge a premium for long-running sessions
items.explain: Ten turns read roughly the sum of one through ten, which is 55 units. Twenty turns read about 210, nearly four times as much.

items.q: Why must limits on an agent run live in code the model cannot reach?
options: Models cannot count their own turns
An instruction to stop is a request; a counter that ends the loop is a limit
Platforms prevent models from reading their own configuration
items.explain: A cap enforced by the same system it is meant to constrain is only a suggestion.

items.q: Why reserve the worst-case budget before a call instead of counting the cost afterwards?
options: Reservations make the provider's invoice smaller
Counting afterwards lets a burst of requests all pass the check together, and the bill arrives anyway
Providers require reservations for any request above a minimum size
items.explain: Reserving first, under a lock, means the burst cannot all pass. The reservation is corrected down to actual use afterwards.

items.q: What bounds everything an agent can do to the world?
options: The instructions in its system prompt
Its list of tools, since it can only act through them
The model's own sense of what is appropriate
items.explain: A model can only produce text. Everything it does beyond that, it does by asking a tool, so the tool list is the set of things that can happen.

items.q: How should you judge whether a tool is safe to give an agent?
options: By how it is intended to be used
By its worst single call with the worst arguments an attacker could choose
By how often it is expected to be called
items.explain: A tool whose worst call you cannot accept is not ready, however well the average call behaves.

items.q: Why is a tool called run_sql described as a hole with a name?
options: It is slower than purpose-built tools
Its worst call is anything the credential permits, so it bounds nothing
Most agent platforms do not support database tools
items.explain: A tool such as get_order_status covers one question and cannot be made to answer another. The general tool covers every question, including ones you never considered.

items.q: Why does a tool's description belong to the security surface?
options: Descriptions are published to the users of the system
The model decides when and how to call the tool from that text, so it shapes behaviour like any prompt
Descriptions determine which credentials a tool may use
items.explain: A vague description invites misuse and a precise one narrows it. Descriptions supplied by third-party services are also text an attacker would like to write.

items.q: A step is right 95% of the time. Roughly how reliable are ten of them in a row?
options: About 95%, since each step is individually reliable
About 60%, because the probabilities multiply down the chain
About 85%, since errors partly cancel each other
items.explain: Ninety-five percent multiplied by itself ten times is about sixty. A demonstration is one run chosen for working; a deployment is thousands of runs.

items.q: Why are early errors in a long run especially damaging?
options: Early steps are more expensive than later ones
Later steps treat earlier output as true and build on it, and nothing downstream can notice
Agents re-run early steps if they detect a fault
items.explain: From where a later step stands, a wrong input looks entirely normal. The run becomes consistent with the mistake.

items.q: What makes a verification step worth having?
options: It uses a more capable model than the step being checked
It checks against something independent of the step being checked, such as a source, a rule or a test
It runs after every single step
items.explain: A model reviewing its own output shares its blind spots. Verification must be able to disagree with what it checks.

items.q: Which change most reliably raises the reliability of a long run?
options: Making each step's prompt longer and more detailed
Removing steps, since every step removed raises the reliability of the whole
Asking the model to double-check its own work at the end
items.explain: A run of five that does the same job as a run of twelve is cheaper and substantially more reliable, which usually beats improving any single step.

items.q: What does an agent remember between turns?
options: Everything it has ever been shown, stored by the model
Only what is in the window it is shown on this turn
Whatever the platform marks as important
items.explain: The model remembers nothing between calls. The history is the memory, so anything trimmed or summarised away no longer exists for it.

items.q: Why is a constraint stated in the first message vulnerable in a long run?
options: Models give less weight to instructions that come first
Summarisation can drop a short sentence from a long history while the summary still reads as complete
Constraints expire after a fixed number of turns
items.explain: Standing rules belong in the system instructions, which are re-sent in full each turn and never summarised.

items.q: In the lesson's phrase, what does the model do and what does your code do about state?
options: The model remembers and your code reasons
The model reasons and your code remembers
Both reason, and neither remembers
items.explain: Anything that must be right, such as how many records are done, should live in a store your code reads, not only as a sentence in the history.

items.q: Why does hostile text fetched early in a run still matter much later?
options: Models keep suspicious text in a separate long-term store
It stays in the window and is re-read on every later turn, so an injection does not expire
Later turns fetch the same page again automatically
items.explain: Read untrusted material in a short-lived sub-task that returns only the facts needed, so the main run never holds the hostile text.

items.q: Why should the completion condition be one that code can check?
options: Models cannot recognise when a task is finished
A model asked whether it has finished tends to say yes, while a mechanical check cannot be talked into agreeing
Checkable conditions run faster than model-judged ones
items.explain: A file existing, a count reached or a test passing does not depend on the model's opinion. Where it cannot be mechanical, the final judgement belongs to a person.

items.q: Which is a cheap, reliable sign that a run is stuck?
options: The model's replies become longer
The same tool called repeatedly with the same arguments
The run takes longer than the previous one
items.explain: Keep recent calls and arguments and end the run if the same pair appears three times. It is a rule, and it works without the model's cooperation.

items.q: A write tool returns 'not permitted'. What should the agent do?
options: Try another tool that achieves the same effect
Stop, and report what it tried and where it stopped
Retry with different arguments until it succeeds
items.explain: When the blockage was put there deliberately, finding a way round is the failure. A refusal should be a stopping condition, not an obstacle.

items.q: Why is an allowlist of permitted actions stronger than a blocklist?
options: Allowlists are quicker to evaluate
A blocklist names what you thought of, and the model finds the thing you did not
Blocklists are not supported by most platforms
items.explain: Only these four tools, only these three folders, only these two domains leaves the model no room for a fifth.

items.q: Why is an agent's final report weak evidence of what it actually did?
options: Agents are instructed to exaggerate their results
It is generated text from the same system that did the work, and may describe an action that never happened
Reports are written before the final steps complete
items.explain: The model writes the most plausible account of a run, and a clean success is more plausible than a messy one. The report tells you where to look; it is not the evidence.

items.q: Why must the trace of a run be written by your code and not by the model?
options: Models cannot produce structured logs
A trace the agent narrates shares the weaknesses of its report, while a log written where the tool is called is a fact
Platforms charge extra for model-generated logs
items.explain: It should also be append-only, so neither the agent nor the tool it calls can edit what it records.

items.q: Which question about a task best predicts whether an agent suits it?
options: Whether the task is currently done by a person
Whether the result can be checked cheaply and independently
Whether the task already involves a language model
items.explain: Errors compound, and the cure is verification that can disagree with the step it checks. Where checking is cheap and mechanical, an agent can try, be told, and try again.

items.q: How should autonomy be introduced into a system?
options: Build the open-ended agent first and constrain it as problems appear
Start with a workflow and promote only the step that genuinely needs a choice, widening as evidence accumulates
Grant full autonomy once a demonstration works reliably
items.explain: Evidence means a trace you have read and a verified success rate. A feeling that it seems to be doing well is not evidence.
